stimuli.text: Initial-rate data for A + B → products:
Initial-rate data for A + B → products:
A student heats 10.2 g of $$\ce{CaCO3(s)}$$, which decomposes completely: $$\ce{CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g)}$$. The $$\ce{CO2}$$ is collected at 293 K and 0.98 atm.
The decomposition of compound X was monitored at constant temperature.
A student titrates 26.0 mL of 0.08 M weak monoprotic acid HA (Ka = 1.4 \times 10^{-4}) with 0.1 M NaOH.
7.1 g of $$\ce{KNO3}$$ dissolves in 115 g of water in a coffee-cup calorimeter. The temperature falls by 9.3 °C. Assume the solution's specific heat is 4.18 J/(g·°C).

A galvanic cell is made of a Zn electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Zn^{2+}}$$ and a Fe electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Fe^{2+}}$$. Standard reduction potentials: $$\ce{Zn^{2+} + 2e- -> Zn}$$ E° = -0.76 V; $$\ce{Fe^{2+} + 2e- -> Fe}$$ E° = -0.44 V.
The photoelectron spectra of Si (Z = 14) and P (Z = 15) are compared.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.02 M solution of $$\ce{HNO3}$$ at 25 °C?

options.why: Correct. Strong acid: [H₃O⁺] equals its concentration.
Strong acids and bases ionize completely; no equilibrium is needed.

questions.stem: Which compound has the greater lattice energy, $$\ce{BaO}$$ or $$\ce{NaF}$$?

options.text: $$\ce{BaO}$$, because its ions have larger charges
options.why: Correct. By Coulomb's law, attraction increases with the product of the ion charges.

options.text: They are equal because both are ionic
$$\ce{NaF}$$, because its ions have larger charges
$$\ce{NaF}$$, because it has more atoms per formula unit
options.why: Number of atoms does not determine lattice energy.

questions.explanation: BaO has ion charges 2 and 2; NaF has 1 and 1.

questions.stem: A 32.7 mL sample of $$\ce{H2SO4}$$ is titrated to the equivalence point with 41.8 mL of 0.269 M NaOH. What is the concentration of the acid?

options.why: Correct. Each H₂SO₄ reacts with two OH⁻, so divide the moles of NaOH by 2.

questions.stem: A weak acid HA has pKa = 7.9. In a solution at pH 10.4, which statement is correct?

options.why: Correct. Above the pKa, the deprotonated form dominates.

questions.stem: Which intermolecular force is present in all molecules?

options.why: Correct. They arise from temporary dipoles in every electron cloud.
Requires H bonded to N, O or F.

questions.explanation: They arise from temporary dipoles in every electron cloud.

questions.stem: Why does I₂ have a higher boiling point than Br₂?

options.why: Boiling does not break covalent bonds.

options.text: I₂ has a larger, more polarizable electron cloud, so stronger London dispersion forces
options.why: Correct. Dispersion forces grow with polarizability.

questions.stem: What volume does 1.19 mol of gas occupy at 1.06 atm and 314 K?

options.why: 22.4 L/mol applies only at 0 °C and 1 atm.
Use R = 0.08206 with atm and L.

questions.stem: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 22.1 g. The actual yield is 14.6 g. What is the percent yield?
A gas mixture contains 0.5 mol N₂, 0.8 mol O₂ and 0.3 mol Ar at a total pressure of 4 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: Use the mole fraction, not moles.
The gases are not present in equal amounts.

questions.stem: Why is the radius of F⁻ larger than that of F?

options.text: F⁻ has an additional electron shell
The added electron increases electron–electron repulsion with the same nuclear charge
options.why: Correct. Anions are larger than their atoms.

questions.explanation: Anions are larger than their atoms.

questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of P in $$\ce{PO4^{3-}}$$?

options.why: Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Correct. The oxidation numbers must sum to the species' overall charge (O usually −2, H usually +1).

questions.stem: A first-order reaction has a half-life of 59 min. Starting at 1.8 M, what is the concentration after 177 min?

options.why: Each half-life halves the concentration; it is not divided by 2n.

questions.stem: A weak acid HA has pKa = 9. In a solution at pH 8.2, which statement is correct?

options.why: Correct. Below the pKa, the protonated form dominates.

questions.stem: Samples of $$\ce{CH4}$$, $$\ce{CO2}$$, $$\ce{Cl2}$$, $$\ce{Ar}$$ are all at the same temperature. Which has the highest average molecular speed?

options.why: Ar has a larger molar mass (40 g/mol).
Cl2 has a larger molar mass (70.9 g/mol).
CO2 has a larger molar mass (44 g/mol).
Correct. At the same temperature, average kinetic energy is equal, so the lightest gas moves fastest.

questions.explanation: Molar masses: CH4 16, CO2 44, Cl2 70.9, Ar 40.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{A(g) + B(g) <=> 2C(g)}$$, K = 9.4. A mixture has [A] = 0.8 M, [B] = 0.7 M and [C] = 0.4 M. In which direction will the reaction proceed?

options.text: It proceeds in reverse, toward reactants, because Q = 0.286
options.why: If Q is less than K, the reaction proceeds forward.

options.text: It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 0.286
options.why: Correct. Q = [C]²/([A][B]) = 0.286, which is less than K.

options.text: It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 0.714
It is at equilibrium, because Q = K

questions.stem: What volume does 0.9 mol of gas occupy at 0.773 atm and 314 K?

options.why: Use R = 0.08206 with atm and L.
22.4 L/mol applies only at 0 °C and 1 atm.

questions.stem: If ΔH = −286 kJ for H₂ + ½O₂ → H₂O(l), what is ΔH for 2H₂O(l) → 2H₂ + O₂?
In a mechanism, a species that is produced in one step and consumed in a later step is a(n):

options.why: Correct. It does not appear in the overall equation.
A catalyst is consumed first and regenerated later.

questions.explanation: It does not appear in the overall equation.

questions.stem: How many valence electrons are shown in the Lewis structure of $$\ce{CO3^{2-}}$$?

options.why: Correct. Sum the valence electrons of all atoms, then add one per negative charge (subtract one per positive charge).

questions.stem: On a reaction energy profile, the reactants are at 43 kJ/mol, the transition state at 128 kJ/mol and the products at 66 kJ/mol. What is ΔH for the reaction?

options.why: Measure from the correct starting point.

questions.explanation: Forward Ea = 85, ΔH = 23, reverse Ea = 62 kJ/mol.

questions.stem: Steel is harder than pure iron because:

options.text: Small carbon atoms in the gaps (interstitial alloy) hinder layers of iron atoms from sliding
Carbon replaces iron atoms of the same size

questions.stem: A reaction has K = 28. What is K for the reaction multiplied by ½?

options.why: Correct. Reverse → 1/K; multiply by n → Kⁿ.
K is raised to a power, not multiplied.
Multiplying by n raises K to the nth power.

questions.stem: Which substance is most soluble in hexane (C₆H₁₄)?

options.why: Ionic compounds dissolve in polar solvents.

questions.stem: Which bond is the most polar?

options.why: Correct. It has the largest electronegativity difference (0.96).

questions.stem: For $$\ce{2N2O5 -> 4NO2 + O2}$$, $$\ce{N2O5}$$ is consumed at 0.01 M/s. At what rate does $$\ce{NO2}$$ form?

options.why: Correct. Multiply by the coefficient ratio 4/2.
Divide by the reactant's coefficient too.

questions.stem: Which indicator is best for titrating acetic acid with NaOH (equivalence pH ≈ 8.7)?

options.why: Correct. Its range includes the equivalence pH.

questions.explanation: Its range includes the equivalence pH.

questions.stem: What is the energy of a photon with a wavelength of 380 nm?

options.why: Correct. E = hc/λ, with λ in meters.

questions.stem: What is the mass percent of C in $$\ce{C2H5OH}$$?

options.why: That is the percent of the other elements.
There are 2 atoms of C in the formula.
Use masses, not numbers of atoms.

questions.stem: 80 mL of 7.4 M solution is diluted to 109 mL. What is the new concentration?

options.why: V₂ is the total final volume.

questions.stem: 143 g of water at 79 °C is mixed with 166 g of water at 14 °C in an insulated container. What is the final temperature?

options.why: Pair each mass with its own temperature.
Correct. Heat lost = heat gained; for water alone, a mass-weighted average.

questions.stem: A photoelectron spectrum shows 6 peaks. From highest to lowest binding energy, their relative heights are 2 : 2 : 6 : 2 : 6 : 2. Which element is it?

options.why: Correct. The peaks correspond to $$1s^{2}\,2s^{2}\,2p^{6}\,3s^{2}\,3p^{6}\,4s^{2}$$, which has 20 electrons.

questions.stem: What is the rate law?

options.why: Recheck how the rate changes when [B] doubles.
Orders are found from the data, not from coefficients.
Correct. Doubling [A] multiplies the rate by 1; doubling [B] multiplies it by 1.
Recheck how the rate changes when [A] doubles.

questions.explanation: Trials 1→2: rate ×1, so order 0 in A. Trials 1→3: rate ×1, so order 0 in B.

questions.stem: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH negative, which change shifts the equilibrium toward NH₃?

options.why: The reaction is exothermic; heating shifts left.
Correct. The product side has fewer moles of gas.

questions.explanation: The product side has fewer moles of gas.

questions.stem: A reaction has K = 47. What is K for the reaction multiplied by 2?

options.why: Correct. Reverse → 1/K; multiply by n → Kⁿ.
K is raised to a power, not multiplied.
Multiplying by n raises K to the nth power.

questions.stem: What is the energy of a photon with a wavelength of 747 nm?

options.why: Correct. E = hc/λ, with λ in meters.

questions.stem: The first four ionization energies of an element are 643, 4501, 7382, 11664 kJ/mol. In which group of the periodic table is the element most likely found?

options.why: Correct. The large jump comes after removing 1 electron, so it has 1 valence electron.
Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.
Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.
Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.

questions.explanation: The big jump marks the start of removing core electrons.

questions.stem: At 298 K, ΔG° for a reaction is -4 kJ/mol. What is K?

options.why: Correct. K = e^(−ΔG°/RT), with ΔG° in J/mol and R = 8.314.

questions.explanation: ln K = 1.61; K = 5.03. Negative ΔG°: K greater than 1.

questions.stem: For a reaction, ΔH° = 101 kJ/mol and ΔS° = -203 J/(mol·K). What is ΔG° at 956 K, and is the reaction favorable?

options.why: Convert ΔS from J to kJ.
Correct. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, with ΔS in kJ/(mol·K).

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.2 M solution of nitrous acid (Ka = 4.5 \times 10^{-4})?

options.why: Correct. Solve Ka = x²/(C − x) for x = [H₃O⁺].
A weak acid does not ionize completely.

questions.stem: A buffer contains 0.19 mol of a weak acid HA (pKa 7.21) and 0.41 mol of its conjugate base A⁻. Then 0.06 mol of NaOH is added. What is the pH?

options.why: Update moles after the added acid or base reacts.
Correct. First react: OH⁻ converts HA to A⁻. Then pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]).

questions.stem: In HCO₃⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CO₃²⁻ + H₃O⁺, which species is the Brønsted–Lowry base?
Is $$\ce{H2O}$$ polar or nonpolar, and why?

options.text: Nonpolar, because it has no polar bonds
options.why: Polarity depends on both bond polarity and geometry.
Containing H does not make a molecule polar.

options.text: Polar, because its bond dipoles do not cancel
Nonpolar, because its bond dipoles cancel by symmetry
options.why: Consider the molecule's shape, not only its bonds.

questions.explanation: H2O is bent; the dipoles do not cancel.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest acid?

options.why: Correct. More oxygen atoms stabilize the conjugate base.

questions.explanation: More oxygen atoms stabilize the conjugate base.

questions.stem: A solution has an absorbance of 0.408 in a 2 cm cuvette. The molar absorptivity is 85 M⁻¹cm⁻¹. What is the concentration?
What is the pressure of 2.43 mol of gas in a 16 L container at 359 K?

options.why: With L and atm, use R = 0.08206.

questions.stem: How many formula units or molecules are in 163 g of $$\ce{H2SO4}$$?

options.why: Correct. Convert grams to moles, then multiply by Avogadro's number.

questions.stem: Which process has a negative ΔS?
The Ksp of $$\ce{CaF2}$$ is 3.9 \times 10^{-11}. What is its molar solubility in pure water?
When a reaction involving 0.062 mol of limiting reactant occurs in 92 g of solution (c = 4.18 J/(g·°C)), the temperature rises by 7.4 °C. What is ΔH for the reaction?

options.why: Correct. q(solution) = mcΔT = 2850 J; q(reaction) = −q(solution); divide by moles.
Divide by the moles of reactant.
A temperature rise means the reaction is exothermic (negative ΔH).

questions.stem: Use the bond enthalpies to estimate ΔH for $$\ce{H2 + Br2 -> 2HBr}$$.

options.why: Bonds formed release energy: subtract them.
Correct. ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed).
Broken minus formed, not formed minus broken.
Multiply each bond energy by the number of bonds.

questions.stem: Reaction 1 has ΔH₁ = -320 kJ and reaction 2 has ΔH₂ = 105 kJ. A target reaction is obtained by doubling reaction 1 and adding reaction 2. What is ΔH for the target reaction?

options.why: Correct. Reverse → change sign; multiply → multiply ΔH; then add.
Reversing changes the sign of ΔH₂.
Enthalpies add; they do not multiply.

questions.stem: A compound (octane) is 84.1% C, 15.9% H by mass. What is its empirical formula?

options.why: That is the molecular formula; reduce to the simplest ratio.
Correct. Convert each percent (in 100 g) to moles and divide by the smallest.

questions.explanation: The mole ratio reduces to C4H9; the molecular formula is C8H18.

questions.stem: Calculate ΔH° for $$\ce{2SO2 + O2 -> 2SO3}$$. (ΔH°f of O₂ is 0.)

options.why: Multiply each ΔH°f by its coefficient.
Correct. Σ n ΔH°f(products) − Σ n ΔH°f(reactants).

questions.stem: For $$\ce{2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl}$$, 45 g of $$\ce{Na}$$ reacts with 86 g of $$\ce{Cl2}$$. What mass of $$\ce{NaCl}$$ can form?

options.why: Apply the mole ratio from the equation.
Not all of both reactants reacts.
Correct. Na is the limiting reactant.
Use the limiting reactant, which gives less product.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g)}$$, initial [H₂] = 0.5 M and [I₂] = 0.6 M, with no HI. At equilibrium, [HI] = 0.4 M. What is K?
For $$\ce{2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl}$$, 97 g of $$\ce{Na}$$ reacts with 87 g of $$\ce{Cl2}$$. What mass of $$\ce{NaCl}$$ can form?

options.why: Apply the mole ratio from the equation.
Correct. Cl2 is the limiting reactant.
Use the limiting reactant, which gives less product.
Not all of both reactants reacts.

questions.stem: A galvanic cell is built from Mg/$$\ce{Mg^{2+}}$$ and Pb/$$\ce{Pb^{2+}}$$ half-cells. Which electrode is the anode?

options.text: Pb, where reduction occurs at the anode
options.why: Reduction occurs at the cathode, not the anode.
The higher potential is reduced at the cathode.
Correct. The half-reaction with the lower reduction potential runs as oxidation at the anode.

questions.explanation: Mg (E° -2.37 V) is oxidized at the anode; Pb is reduced at the cathode.

questions.stem: A galvanic cell is built from Mg/$$\ce{Mg^{2+}}$$ and Al/$$\ce{Al^{3+}}$$ half-cells. Which electrode is the anode?

options.why: Correct. The half-reaction with the lower reduction potential runs as oxidation at the anode.

options.text: Al, where reduction occurs at the anode
options.why: Reduction occurs at the cathode, not the anode.
The higher potential is reduced at the cathode.

questions.explanation: Mg (E° -2.37 V) is oxidized at the anode; Al is reduced at the cathode.

questions.stem: A weak acid (pKa 4.87) is titrated with NaOH; the equivalence point is reached at 27.1 mL. What is the pH after 13.6 mL of NaOH has been added?

options.why: That is only for strong acid–strong base equivalence.
Correct. At the half-equivalence point, [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa.

questions.stem: What is the rate law?

options.why: Orders are found from the data, not from coefficients.
Recheck how the rate changes when [A] doubles.
Compare trials where only one concentration changes.
Correct. Doubling [A] multiplies the rate by 2; doubling [B] multiplies it by 1.

questions.explanation: Trials 1→2: rate ×2, so order 1 in A. Trials 1→3: rate ×1, so order 0 in B.

parts.prompt: Calculate the number of moles of CO₂ produced.

rubric.criterion: Correct moles using molar mass 100.09 g/mol and the 1:1 ratio.

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of CO₂ expected.
The student measures 2.35 L of gas. Calculate the percent yield, and give one experimental reason the yield could be less than 100%.

rubric.example: Incomplete decomposition (not heated long enough) or gas leaking from the apparatus.

parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a complete Lewis diagram for CO₂, and identify its molecular geometry and the hybridization of carbon.

rubric.example: O=C=O with two lone pairs on each O (16 valence electrons).

parts.prompt: Explain why CO₂ is nonpolar even though C=O bonds are polar.

rubric.criterion: Linear symmetry makes the bond dipoles cancel.

parts.prompt: CaO is an ionic solid. Explain, using Coulomb's law, why CaO has a higher melting point than KCl.

rubric.criterion: Larger ion charges in CaO (2+/2−) than in KCl (1+/1−).
Greater electrostatic attraction (and smaller ions) means more energy is needed to separate the ions.

parts.prompt: Calculate the average rate of disappearance of X between 0 and 20 s.
Determine the order of the reaction with respect to X. Justify your answer using the data.

rubric.example: Equal time intervals give equal changes in ln[X].

parts.prompt: Write the rate law and determine the rate constant, with units.
Calculate the half-life of the reaction (for the initial concentration).
A proposed mechanism has a slow first step: X → Y + Z. Is the mechanism consistent with the rate law? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Yes; the slow step's elementary rate law matches the observed rate law.

parts.prompt: A catalyst is added. Explain its effect on the rate and on the rate constant, using activation energy.

rubric.example: The catalyst provides a new pathway.

rubric.criterion: Lower activation energy means a larger fraction of collisions are successful.

parts.prompt: Write the net ionic equation for the titration reaction.
Calculate the initial pH of the acid solution.

rubric.criterion: Ka expression set up with x = [H₃O⁺].

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of NaOH needed to reach the equivalence point.
What is the pH at the half-equivalence point? Justify.
Calculate the pH at the equivalence point.

rubric.criterion: Uses Kb = Kw/Ka and the diluted [A⁻].

parts.prompt: Choose an appropriate indicator from: methyl orange (pKa 3.7), bromothymol blue (pKa 7.0), phenolphthalein (pKa 9.3). Justify.

rubric.criterion: Indicator whose pKa is closest to the equivalence pH.

parts.prompt: Explain why the solution at the half-equivalence point resists pH change when a small amount of HCl is added.

rubric.criterion: A⁻ reacts with added H⁺ to form HA (buffer).
rubric.example: A⁻ + H₃O⁺ → HA + H₂O, so the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] changes only slightly.

parts.prompt: Is the dissolution endothermic or exothermic? Justify.

rubric.example: Endothermic: the solution cooled, so energy was absorbed.

parts.prompt: Calculate the heat absorbed or released by the solution.
Calculate ΔH of dissolution in kJ/mol.
If some heat escaped to the surroundings, would the magnitude of the calculated ΔH be too large or too small? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Too small, because the measured temperature change is smaller than the true change.

parts.prompt: Write the balanced net ionic equation for the cell reaction.
Calculate E°cell.
Calculate ΔG° for the cell reaction.
The concentration of Zn²⁺ is increased to 2.0 M. Predict the effect on the cell potential and justify.

rubric.criterion: E decreases because Q increases (a product's concentration rises).
rubric.example: Q greater than 1 → E less than E°.

questions.title: Solubility of a slightly soluble salt

parts.prompt: Write the Ksp expression.
Calculate the molar solubility in pure water.
Calculate the molar solubility in a solution containing 0.01 M F⁻ (from a soluble salt).
Explain how lowering the pH affects the solubility.

rubric.criterion: Correct reasoning about whether the anion is basic.
rubric.example: Solubility increases: H⁺ reacts with F⁻ (a base), shifting the equilibrium toward dissolving.

parts.prompt: Write the electron configuration of P.
Explain why the 1s peak of P has a higher binding energy than the 1s peak of Si.

rubric.criterion: P has more protons, so 1s electrons are attracted more strongly (Coulomb's law).

parts.prompt: Describe one difference in the number or relative height of peaks between the two spectra.

rubric.criterion: A valid difference based on configurations.
rubric.example: P has one more electron, so its outermost peak is taller or an extra peak appears.

parts.prompt: Which element has the larger atomic radius? Justify using Coulomb's law.

rubric.criterion: Si: fewer protons with similar shielding, so valence electrons are held less tightly.
rubric.example: Same period; effective nuclear charge increases across.
